table.text: We recruited 316 novice raters through Prolific (age: M = 36.32, SD = 11.73, range = 18-84; gender: 191 M, 107 F, 6 unspecified; ethnicity: 197 White/Caucasian, 35 Asian, 24 Black/African American, 17 Hispanic/Latino, 1 American Indian/Alaska Native, 30 other; language: native = 294, fluent = 10; 12 excluded due to data quality issues).

ethics_check.report:
Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

> All participants were fluent or native adult English speakers, located in the United States, with normal or corrected-to-normal hearing and vision, and access to a computer in a quiet environment.

> All participants gave informed consent before starting the study.

> In total, we originally recruited 100 storytellers via Prolific (https://prolific.com) to generate 6 stories each.

> We recruited 316 novice raters through Prolific (age: M = 36.32, SD = 11.73, range = 18-84; gender: 191 M, 107 F, 6 unspecified; ethnicity: 197 White/Caucasian, 35 Asian, 24 Black/African American, 17 Hispanic/Latino, 1 American Indian/Alaska Native, 30 other; language: native = 294, fluent = 10; 12 excluded due to data quality issues).

> In contrast, a multi-session design was less suitable for novice raters, who were recruited online to maintain a diverse and heterogeneous participant pool.

> Multi-session online studies are associated with higher attrition rates (Rodd, 2024), and based on our lab's prior experience it would have been very difficult to find online participants through Prolific to complete all sessions.

> Likewise, some storytellers (even within the general population sampled in our Prolific pool) may be consistently more creative than others, and follow-up work could search for common narrative strategies or structural patterns that distinguish or cluster these storytellers based on their baseline or default level of creativity.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.header: Minimal influence of expertise on the overall structure of the story rating space

table.formatted: We found no significant main effect of rater group on overall ratings across dimensions (β = -0.12, SE = 0.15, p = 0.424) (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref>).
table.header: Minimal influence of expertise on the overall structure of the story rating space
table.expanded: We found no significant main effect of rater group on overall ratings across dimensions (β = -0.12, SE = 0.15, p = 0.424) (Figure 1A).

table.header: Minimal influence of expertise on the overall structure of the story rating space
table.expanded: In contrast, the two groups' ratings did not differ significantly for creativity (β = -0.05, SE = 0.16, p = 0.732), imagination (β = -0.07, SE = 0.16, p = 0.673), novelty (β = -0.09, SE = 0.16, p = 0.582), or cohesiveness (β = 0.12, SE = 0.16, p = 0.423) (All five post-hoc tests above were Bonferroni corrected).

table.header: Minimal influence of expertise on the overall structure of the story rating space
table.expanded: In contrast, the two groups' ratings did not differ significantly for creativity (β = -0.05, SE = 0.16, p = 0.732), imagination (β = -0.07, SE = 0.16, p = 0.673), novelty (β = -0.09, SE = 0.16, p = 0.582), or cohesiveness (β = 0.12, SE = 0.16, p = 0.423) (All five post-hoc tests above were Bonferroni corrected).

table.header: Minimal influence of expertise on the overall structure of the story rating space
table.expanded: In contrast, the two groups' ratings did not differ significantly for creativity (β = -0.05, SE = 0.16, p = 0.732), imagination (β = -0.07, SE = 0.16, p = 0.673), novelty (β = -0.09, SE = 0.16, p = 0.582), or cohesiveness (β = 0.12, SE = 0.16, p = 0.423) (All five post-hoc tests above were Bonferroni corrected).

table.header: Minimal influence of expertise on the overall structure of the story rating space
table.expanded: In contrast, the two groups' ratings did not differ significantly for creativity (β = -0.05, SE = 0.16, p = 0.732), imagination (β = -0.07, SE = 0.16, p = 0.673), novelty (β = -0.09, SE = 0.16, p = 0.582), or cohesiveness (β = 0.12, SE = 0.16, p = 0.423) (All five post-hoc tests above were Bonferroni corrected).

As predicted, stories that had higher word and sentence counts were rated as more creative (β = 0.10, SE = 0.04, p = 0.006; β = 0.08, SE = 0.04, p = 0.039, respectively) but not more cohesive (β = 0.05, SE = 0.03, p = 0.184; β = -0.03, SE = 0.03, p = 0.422, respectively).

As predicted, stories that had higher word and sentence counts were rated as more creative (β = 0.10, SE = 0.04, p = 0.006; β = 0.08, SE = 0.04, p = 0.039, respectively) but not more cohesive (β = 0.05, SE = 0.03, p = 0.184; β = -0.03, SE = 0.03, p = 0.422, respectively).
On the other hand, stories with longer MLU were rated as more cohesive but not more creative (β = 0.08, SE = 0.03, p = 0.016; β = 0.002, SE = 0.04, p = 0.942, respectively).

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. report: This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.
We examined 1 codebook/README/label source and 1050 data columns across 16 files.
No codebook or README documentation was found, so no data columns could be matched to variable definitions.
#### Duplicated Column Names

- **Duplicated column names in `novice_survey.csv`.** 1 column name appears more than once (worst: `Rec_Session_Id`×2), so 2 of the file's 73 columns share a name with another. This usually means a survey loop/merge exported repeated blocks without numbering each iteration; the repeats cannot be told apart and can only be documented once. Consider re-exporting with per-iteration column names.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 1050 columns across 16 data files.
#### Issues Identified

62 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

**About the personal-information flags.** These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

- **Column names** are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (`email`, `telefoonnummer`, `geboortedatum`, ...). A column called `phone_number` flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
- **Values** are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
- **Free text** is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means *look at this column*. Where the data is already de-identified (an `ip` column reading `Anonymized`, a `name` column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

#### Careless Responding

43 distinct respondents were flagged for **straightlining**: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is **one row per person**, and the *Longest run* column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, **43 were flagged *only* by short-scale straightlining** (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.
These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

**What this does not cover.** Only 1 of 16 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

findings.detail: 1 value with leading/trailing whitespace: "I've taken courses in creative writing and composed creative pieces. It's been haphazard, but intensive work between the ages of ~8 and ~14, work in class contexts, workshop contexts, and literary magazine contexts ~14-21, and no recent creative writing work. 8-14 = short stories, older = poetry and occasional short stories. "

3 values with leading/trailing whitespace: "A written work with a narrative arc. It must in some way manipulate events / facts / fiction. It may be based in non-fiction or ""true"" events, but to be creative, it must embroider, develop, or otherwise change how it presents those events to some extent. ", "A creative story is a story where at least one factor of the story is fictional. The story should have a setting, character(s), and sequence of event(s) relating to the character(s). A creative story should be written by a human and not by a computer, machine or artificial intelligence. ", "A story that contains elements I have not seen or heard before.  A story that is immersive in both imagery and sequence so that I want to keep listening or reading it.  A story that makes me think, or I keep thinking about it after I have finished it.  A story that contains a twist or surprise I did not see coming.  I am the type of reader who visualizes what I am reading.  I ""go through' the page and ""watch the movie"" the words are producing.  If I can do that easily, the story is creative.        "

5 values with leading/trailing whitespace: "How much (or little) the rhetorical choices (details, frame, development) manipulate true, or fictionalized events. ", "A plot that is well thought out and the characters are really built up. It must have elements that provoke emotional connectivity to the reader. ", "1. If a story is a description or retelling of a real event with no creative creation, it is not a creative story. 
2. A creative story has to have certain fictional elements that originated from the author. For example, the author must have created a character, or specific creative interpretation of a real individual. 
3. A creative story should not plagiarize another story. ", "If I find it engaging. If it's predictable I will get bored or become uninterested.  I have a short list of authors that I know produce creative work, and sometimes I will read other authors that they recommend.  Like I said on the last question, the ability to easily ""construct the movie"" in my minds eye as I read is a hallmark of creativity I look for.  ", "I think when telling a story it must come across as very authentic in the structure of the story this allows it to be accepted as believable. When we consider storytelling we only need to look at the truthful amazing stories we have heard from friends, associates, and strangers we have conversed with over our life span. That said being imaginative and creative within the storytelling aspect is key for creating a compelling experience remember facts tell story sells. Storytelling at the highest level implements these elements while allowing the creator to pour some of their being within the story-telling process no matter how short or lengthy the story. Many people cook with an exact recipe but the best cooks only cook with that innate ability to know this will taste amazing from instinctual guidance that is spontaneous and organic. It changes with the mood of the soul as what is happening takes place in the moment like a painter at the beach or on a busy street corner. There is an invisible energy that wishes to have its turn at the dance of expression. "

5 values with leading/trailing whitespace: "I think all these are relevant in assessing creativity ", "I'm not sure if imagination is always required in assessing the creativity of a story. Imagining new creatures or new scenarios does not always make a story creative. A story can be creative without being very imaginative. ", "Cohesiveness was an automatic high number if the story had a beginning, middle, and end with believable linkages knitting them together.  Novelty is good, but I thought it in terms of originality.  Imagination was harder to assess.  Many of these stories read like memories which means they were not created but remembered and modified.  Complexity is an element hard to assess when you are dealing with stories created in a three minute time limit.  Common tropes emerged (the ghost stories) probably because those are themes common to nearly everyone and were easy to access quickly.  Complexity requires depth, and perhaps depth requires time.  Reading these stories was like watching an improv group trying to generate a narrative from random objects yelled out by the audience.    ", "These are good dimensions.  ", "I think all of these dimensions are relevant to assess story creativity. However, I found myself not being entirely sure how to evaluate ""novelty"" as the study progressed. Was I supposed to rate the story as novel in general, or novel given the clear common factors across many of these stories? I also think that, when I consider a story creative, its novelty isn't necessarily the most strongly weighted component...depending on what the novelty consists of, I suppose. So, for example novel settings vs places vs characters vs plot points may change how creative I perceive a story more or less. I think the relationship between expected plot points and unexpected plot points / details probably has the strongest bearing on my understanding of creativity. There can be a simple but creative story as well; complex details tended, to me, to suggest a more imaginative story because they fleshed out character/setting/plot more. I found these things seemed to correlate and sometimes I had trouble distinguishing the two when I was rating because complexity felt so causal to imagination. Cohesion seemed to relate more to my satisfaction as a reader and my ability to see a strong (or weak) arc to the narrative. I think many creative stories don't have to be cohesive; I do think that many cohesive stories aren't necessarily creative. I could see some correlation here, but it felt like there was a very different relationship between cohesion and creativity in these stories than in say imagination / complexity and creativity. "

6 values with leading/trailing whitespace: "Dimension. The dimension of the characters and the world is vital in creative story telling. ", "I think the ultimate theme or idea is important in a story. I think that comes out of all the elements and how they fit together at the end. If there's not an idea, then there's no point to the story. With that also, I think a good story has pacing and builds to a climax. ", "I wish I could have heard them speaking their stories.  The mood the speakers were trying to covey, and their attitudes towards their own stories would have been a little more clear.  The clarity would have helped me past the language, grammar, and spelling issues.    ", " I would add something to recognize quality of detail. ", "character (whether that is human or not), plot points/development, details, and audience expectations all seemed really critical to me during the study and in my general sense of creative storytelling. A story about a princess in a tower with a dragon isn't really creative necessarily, but Shrek really was because of how it played with audience expectations, imo. Some of the more creative stories drew on common elements of the study but interpreted them in neat ways, with more fleshed out identities/motivations for characters and more interesting changes in use of plot points/details. ", "I don't think so "

live_data_statements: All participants were fluent or native adult English speakers, located in the United States, with normal or corrected-to-normal hearing and vision, and access to a computer in a quiet environment.
All participants gave informed consent before starting the study.
In total, we originally recruited 100 storytellers via Prolific (https://prolific.com) to generate 6 stories each.

We recruited 316 novice raters through Prolific (age: M = 36.32, SD = 11.73, range = 18-84; gender: 191 M, 107 F, 6 unspecified; ethnicity: 197 White/Caucasian, 35 Asian, 24 Black/African American, 17 Hispanic/Latino, 1 American Indian/Alaska Native, 30 other; language: native = 294, fluent = 10; 12 excluded due to data quality issues).
In contrast, a multi-session design was less suitable for novice raters, who were recruited online to maintain a diverse and heterogeneous participant pool.

Multi-session online studies are associated with higher attrition rates (Rodd, 2024), and based on our lab's prior experience it would have been very difficult to find online participants through Prolific to complete all sessions.

Likewise, some storytellers (even within the general population sampled in our Prolific pool) may be consistently more creative than others, and follow-up work could search for common narrative strategies or structural patterns that distinguish or cluster these storytellers based on their baseline or default level of creativity.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 4 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(Order = 1:4, File = c("analysis + figures v6.Rmd", 
"analysis + figures.Rmd", "demographics.Rmd", "prepare dataset.Rmd"
), "Runs after" = c("—", "—", "—", "—"), Basis = c("numeric", 
"none", "none", "none")), row.names = c(NA, -4L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```
#### File paths
Every data path in the code works in the repository as deposited.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 4 scripts: 3 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

```{r}

# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("analysis + figures v6.Rmd", "analysis + figures.Rmd", 
"demographics.Rmd", "prepare dataset.Rmd"), Outcome = c("ran_ok", 
"errored", "ran_ok", "ran_ok"), Detail = c("", "undefined_variable", 
"", ""), "Time (s)" = c(45, 38.6, 2.1, 24.3)), row.names = c(NA, 
-4L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**Undefined-variable errors**

**1 script failed on an undefined variable or function** (`object '...' not found` / `could not find function "..."`). This typically means the script expects a variable or function that another script defines — i.e. it is meant to be sourced into a larger session, not run on its own — or the symbol is simply never created. When another of the paper's own script files defines the same name, this is called out below as a likely sourcing/copy-paste gap. Each is counted as an error (red).

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = "analysis + figures.Rmd", "Missing variable" = "PC1", 
    "Defined in" = "(not defined anywhere in the paper's code)"), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```

This module also assesses whether the paper's Python code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 4 Python code files.
#### Run order

The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first) and numeric filename prefixes. Python has no `source()`-equivalent import-based ordering signal (an `import` loads a module, not the paper's own analysis flow), so that basis never applies here.

#### File paths

#### Execution

**The Python code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 4 scripts: 0 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 1 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 0 are written for Python 2 and not run. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions (e.g. in a `requirements.txt`). **3 scripts need the internet**, which is off during the run: gpt2_surprisal_entropy.ipynb, longformer raw embeddings + metrics.ipynb, sentiment analysis.ipynb. text.formatted: The raw and processed datasets, scripts for data preprocessing, wrangling, analysis, and figures (R and Python) are available at OSF: <ref type="url" target="https://osf.io/qzsy3/?view_only=7c75e8804ebc40c78e19cfb4c282eb5b">https://osf.io/qzsy3/?view_only=7c75e8804ebc40c78e19cfb4c282eb5b</ref>.

text.text: This study has been submitted as an abstract and presented as talks and posters at several conferences and workshops.
The perception of creative works is inherently subjective and varies widely across the human population.
The same contemporary painting or novel might be considered a deeply moving masterpiece to some but unappealing or mundane to others.
How do different people arrive at these diverse judgments?
Are there systematic patterns underlying these divergent opinions?

These questions remain poorly understood but are worth studying, since creative works-much like political beliefs and other potentially polarizing subjects-offer a valuable window into the complexity of human judgment and perception.

To rigorously study human aesthetic judgment, as well as its relation to other cognitive abilities (e.g., visual perception), and its practical applications in education, product design, and marketing (Serban et al., 2023; Sarkar & Chakrabarti, 2011), requires developing valid and reliable methods of assessment.
text.formatted: To rigorously study human aesthetic judgment, as well as its relation to other cognitive abilities (e.g., visual perception), and its practical applications in education, product design, and marketing <ref type="bibr" target="#b81">(Serban et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b79">Sarkar & Chakrabarti, 2011)</ref>, requires developing valid and reliable methods of assessment.

text.text: The Consensual Assessment Technique (CAT, Amabile, 1982) has been particularly influential for this purpose, especially in the domain of creativity.
text.formatted: The Consensual Assessment Technique (CAT, <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Amabile, 1982)</ref> has been particularly influential for this purpose, especially in the domain of creativity.

text.text: In this method, experts from a specific field rate creative works along one or more dimensions (e.g., creativity, novelty, imagination) using their own subjective definitions.
This approach relies on the "wisdom of experts"; that is, the general consensus among experts, regardless of their underlying reasoning, is treated as ground truth.
However, reducing a multitude of ratings to a concise score summarizing experts' opinion overlooks the vast variability in human perception.

Thus, rather than relying on expert consensus to represent the "ideal" of human creative perception, a contrasting line of research has explored individual differences in aesthetic judgments (Jacobsen & Höfel, 2002; Street et al., 2016; Celikors & Field, 2025) shaped by personal, social, and educational factors.
text.formatted: Thus, rather than relying on expert consensus to represent the "ideal" of human creative perception, a contrasting line of research has explored individual differences in aesthetic judgments <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Jacobsen & Höfel, 2002;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b84">Street et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Celikors & Field, 2025)</ref> shaped by personal, social, and educational factors.

text.text: For instance, personality influences the leniency of creativity ratings (Tan et al., 2015), and social identity biases raters to perceive ideas generated by members from the same social group as more creative (Adarves-Yorno et al., 2008).
text.formatted: For instance, personality influences the leniency of creativity ratings <ref type="bibr" target="#b85">(Tan et al., 2015)</ref>, and social identity biases raters to perceive ideas generated by members from the same social group as more creative <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Adarves-Yorno et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Academics from different disciplines (e.g., natural sciences vs. humanities) define the originality of scholarship in distinct ways (Guetzkow et al., 2004).
text.formatted: Academics from different disciplines (e.g., natural sciences vs. humanities) define the originality of scholarship in distinct ways <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Guetzkow et al., 2004)</ref>.

text.text: Additionally, the weighting of different dimensions (e.g., novelty vs. appropriateness) in assessments of overall quality of creative products differs across cultures (Paletz & Peng, 2008).
text.formatted: Additionally, the weighting of different dimensions (e.g., novelty vs. appropriateness) in assessments of overall quality of creative products differs across cultures <ref type="bibr" target="#b68">(Paletz & Peng, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: One major source of variability in how people perceive, interpret, and evaluate complex stimuli is expertise.

Cognitive scientists have conceptualized expertise from several perspectives, including the accumulation of domain-specific knowledge (through extensive training and practice) that refines perceptual sensitivity and pattern recognition, and the flexible application of knowledge to novel and complex situations (Farrington-Darby & Wilson, 2006).
text.formatted: Cognitive scientists have conceptualized expertise from several perspectives, including the accumulation of domain-specific knowledge (through extensive training and practice) that refines perceptual sensitivity and pattern recognition, and the flexible application of knowledge to novel and complex situations <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Farrington-Darby & Wilson, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Domain expertise has been shown to influence ratings of the originality of visual art (Celikors & Field, 2025), poetry (Kaufman et al., 2008; Chaudhuri et al., 2024a; 2024b), and mathematical equations (Hayn-Leichsenring et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Domain expertise has been shown to influence ratings of the originality of visual art <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Celikors & Field, 2025)</ref>, poetry <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">(Kaufman et al., 2008;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Chaudhuri et al., 2024a;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2024b)</ref>, and mathematical equations <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Hayn-Leichsenring et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Here, we focus on improvised oral storytelling, a form of creative expression that is more universal and accessible than these other art forms.
Stories are ubiquitous in everyday life, in the novels, news articles, and videos we consume, and in conversations we exchange with our friends.

Thus, even without formal training, most people have extensive experience with storytelling, through which they may have generated implicit interpretive frameworks that inform their subjective evaluation of stories.

Therefore, this medium provides a valuable opportunity to test how formal expertise differs from everyday experience, in contrast to prior work on poetry or mathematical equations, with which most people may have very limited experience.

Research investigating mechanisms of creativity perception of improvised oral stories is exceedingly rare, but a few studies have addressed the influence of expertise on creativity assessment of written short stories, finding that average creativity ratings differ relatively little between experts and novices (Kaufman et al., 2009) and that experts' and novices' ratings are strongly correlated (Taylor et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Research investigating mechanisms of creativity perception of improvised oral stories is exceedingly rare, but a few studies have addressed the influence of expertise on creativity assessment of written short stories, finding that average creativity ratings differ relatively little between experts and novices <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">(Kaufman et al., 2009)</ref> and that experts' and novices' ratings are strongly correlated <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">(Taylor et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: However, it should be noted that the latter of these used "creativity researchers" as experts (instead of storytellers or writers), who also likely differed significantly in age from the undergraduate "novices", and also included only three raters per group.

Furthermore, prior work has not fully taken advantage of the rich, dynamic linguistic structure of stories, which may offer deeper insights into how training in storytelling or creative writing may confer heightened or shifted sensitivity to certain structural dimensions more than others, even when overall ratings appear to be similar on the surface.

To answer this question, we measured linguistic features of human-generated stories from four diverse categories: semantic similarity, lexical predictability, lexical composition, and language productivity.

These categories capture distinct aspects of linguistic information that have been investigated across diverse paradigms in story and text processing (elaborated below; e.g., Johnson et al., 2022; Laurino Dos Santos & Berger, 2022; Willems et al., 2016; Min & Park, 2019).
text.formatted: These categories capture distinct aspects of linguistic information that have been investigated across diverse paradigms in story and text processing (elaborated below; e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Johnson et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b53">Laurino Dos Santos & Berger, 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Willems et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b59">Min & Park, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: However, previous studies have typically focused on a limited subset of linguistic features, often examining them in isolation or within specific theoretical frameworks.
Here, we adopt a more integrative approach by examining multiple categories of linguistic elements, which allows us to assess their relative and complementary contributions to narrative evaluation.

The semantic similarity category is based on a comparison between embeddings, or vectorized multidimensional representations that reflect semantic relatedness between words (e.g., "ball" and "soccer" have higher similarity than "ball" and "cake").

Metrics derived from this concept have emerged as prominent predictors of creativity across tasks (AUT, word association; Heinen & Johnson et al., 2018; Beaty & Johnson, 2021; short stories; Johnson et al., 2022), based on the principle that creative thinking involves connecting distantly related concepts (Mednick, 1962; Beaty & Kenett, 2023).
text.formatted: Metrics derived from this concept have emerged as prominent predictors of creativity across tasks (AUT, word association; <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Heinen & Johnson et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Beaty & Johnson, 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr">short stories;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Johnson et al., 2022)</ref>, based on the principle that creative thinking involves connecting distantly related concepts <ref type="bibr" target="#b62">(Mednick, 1962;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">Beaty & Kenett, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Semantic similarity based on context-dependent word embeddings has been shown to reliably predict human creativity ratings of short stories (lower average semantic similarity across all words predicts higher creativity; Johnson et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Semantic similarity based on context-dependent word embeddings has been shown to reliably predict human creativity ratings of short stories (lower average semantic similarity across all words predicts higher creativity; <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Johnson et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Here, we build on this line of work by using Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020), a transformer model that generates contextualized embeddings (i.e., dynamic representations that integrate prior semantic context) across much longer passages than previous models (e.g., BERT; Devlin et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Here, we build on this line of work by using Longformer <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Beltagy et al., 2020)</ref>, a transformer model that generates contextualized embeddings (i.e., dynamic representations that integrate prior semantic context) across much longer passages than previous models (e.g., BERT; <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Devlin et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: We included well-established measures of word-and sentence-level semantic similarity across levels of granularity and temporal scope (e.g., average similarity across all word or sentence pairs, or across all adjacent sentence pairs; Johnson et al., 2022; Reilly et al., 2023; Toubia et al., 2021 , Skalicky et al., 2017) as well as a novel first-to-last sentence similarity measure that captures the global accumulation of semantic information across an entire story.
text.formatted: We included well-established measures of word-and sentence-level semantic similarity across levels of granularity and temporal scope (e.g., average similarity across all word or sentence pairs, or across all adjacent sentence pairs; <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Johnson et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b75">Reilly et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b87">Toubia et al., 2021</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b82">, Skalicky et al., 2017)</ref> as well as a novel first-to-last sentence similarity measure that captures the global accumulation of semantic information across an entire story.

text.text: Next, we measured lexical predictability (surprisal and entropy), drawing on surprisal theory in sentence processing, which links comprehension difficulty under cognitive constraints to the probability of linguistic input given prior context (Hale, 2001; Levy, 2008).
text.formatted: Next, we measured lexical predictability (surprisal and entropy), drawing on surprisal theory in sentence processing, which links comprehension difficulty under cognitive constraints to the probability of linguistic input given prior context <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Hale, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">Levy, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: These measures have been shown to predict behavioral indices of language processing (e.g., reading time slowdowns : Smith & Levy, 2013; Lowder et al., 2018; Aurnhammer & Frank, 2019), as well as neural responses in ERP and fMRI studies (Frank et al., 2015; Willems et al., 2016).
text.formatted: These measures have been shown to predict behavioral indices of language processing (e.g., reading time slowdowns <ref type="bibr" target="#b83">: Smith & Levy, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">Lowder et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Aurnhammer & Frank, 2019)</ref>, as well as neural responses in ERP and fMRI studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Frank et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b91">Willems et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Words that have high surprisal in a particular context are less predictable in that context and tend to be more difficult to process.
Entropy captures the overall uncertainty associated with predicting the next token, and high entropy positions have many other similarly likely alternatives following previous text.

The dual-metric approach to information-theoretic measures provides complementary insights: surprisal measures token-specific predictability, while entropy captures overall model uncertainty at each prediction point.

Our third category, lexical composition, also operates at the word level but focuses more directly on the semantic and content-related properties of language than on its abstract statistical predictability.

Specifically, it includes the number of lexical categories (reflecting lexical diversity) contained in a story, the sentiment (emotionality) of words, and the number of story elements provided in the prompt (reflecting improvisational constraints).

Lexical diversity has been found to predict creativity ratings of stories (Kandemirci et al., 2025) and it has been suggested that more constraints might generate more creativity (Tromp & Baer, 2022).
text.formatted: Lexical diversity has been found to predict creativity ratings of stories <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Kandemirci et al., 2025)</ref> and it has been suggested that more constraints might generate more creativity <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Tromp & Baer, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: However, these features have not been looked at together, and their relationship with other story dimensions and expertise effect has not been examined.
Finally, we included measures of language productivity (e.g., word count, readability), as coarse indicators of baseline verbal fluency.
Several studies have found word count to be a robust predictor of narrative creativity (Taylor et al., 2021; Johnson et al., 2022; Forthmann et al., 2018; Kandemirci et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Several studies have found word count to be a robust predictor of narrative creativity <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">(Taylor et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Johnson et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Forthmann et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Kandemirci et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Consistent with previous work (Johnson et al., 2022), we used them primarily as control variables to account for general differences in verbal output when evaluating metrics from the other three categories.
text.formatted: Consistent with previous work <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Johnson et al., 2022)</ref>, we used them primarily as control variables to account for general differences in verbal output when evaluating metrics from the other three categories.

text.text: This would allow us to assess whether the other linguistic features explained variation in story evaluations beyond what could be attributed to differences in the sheer quantity of language produced.
The present study targets two questions regarding human evaluation of improvised spoken stories.
First, we asked how expertise in storytelling and creative writing shapes ratings of different story dimensions: creativity, imagination, novelty, complexity, and cohesiveness.

To capture multiple aspects of narratives while keeping the rating task manageable, we selected these dimensions based on prior empirical and theoretical work, which suggested that they capture complementary and distinct aspects of narrative evaluation (e.g., Hennessey & Amabile, 1988; Amabile, 1982; Runco & Jaeger, 2012; Graesser et al., 2011).
text.formatted: To capture multiple aspects of narratives while keeping the rating task manageable, we selected these dimensions based on prior empirical and theoretical work, which suggested that they capture complementary and distinct aspects of narrative evaluation (e.g., Hennessey <ref type="bibr">& Amabile, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Amabile, 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Runco & Jaeger, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Graesser et al., 2011)</ref>.

text.text: Creativity, novelty, imagination, and complexity have been examined in prior work on creative evaluation (Hennessey & Amabile, 1988; Amabile, 1982).
text.formatted: Creativity, novelty, imagination, and complexity have been examined in prior work on creative evaluation <ref type="bibr">(Hennessey & Amabile, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Amabile, 1982)</ref>.

text.text: Cohesiveness broadly covers other rubric items included in these same studies (e.g., logic and organization), and it has been investigated more directly in research on discourse coherence and comprehension (e.g., Foltz et al., 1998; Graesser et al., 2011; McNamara et al., 2010; Crossley, 2020).
text.formatted: Cohesiveness broadly covers other rubric items included in these same studies (e.g., logic and organization), and it has been investigated more directly in research on discourse coherence and comprehension (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Foltz et al., 1998;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Graesser et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b61">McNamara et al., 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Crossley, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: We predicted that across both groups, these ratings would collapse into two main components (roughly, creativity and cohesiveness) (Patel et al., 2025).
text.formatted: We predicted that across both groups, these ratings would collapse into two main components (roughly, creativity and cohesiveness) <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">(Patel et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: However, we also predicted that experts' training and extended practice might fine-tune their conceptualization of different dimensions (e.g., creativity vs. novelty), causing them to perceive them as more nuanced and independent from each other.
Second, we asked how expertise impacts the influence of four diverse categories of linguistic features (described above) on these ratings.
Across both groups, we expect lower semantic similarity (between words or between sentences) to predict higher creativity (as in Johnson et al., 2022), but lower cohesiveness (Foltz et al., 1998).
text.formatted: Across both groups, we expect lower semantic similarity (between words or between sentences) to predict higher creativity (as in <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Johnson et al., 2022)</ref>, but lower cohesiveness <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Foltz et al., 1998)</ref>.

text.text: Similarly, we expect that stories with higher surprisal (and potentially, higher entropy) will be rated as more creative or novel (Filipowicz, 2006), but less cohesive, due to the added processing difficulty (Lowder et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Similarly, we expect that stories with higher surprisal (and potentially, higher entropy) will be rated as more creative or novel <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Filipowicz, 2006)</ref>, but less cohesive, due to the added processing difficulty <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Lowder et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: In terms of lexical composition, prior work has found links between the intensity of sentiment of stories and creativity ratings (Hoffmann et al., 2024), but other linguistic features in this category have not been well-studied.
text.formatted: In terms of lexical composition, prior work has found links between the intensity of sentiment of stories and creativity ratings <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Hoffmann et al., 2024)</ref>, but other linguistic features in this category have not been well-studied.

text.text: Here, we predict that more creative stories may have greater lexical diversity, more lexical categories, and more intense sentiment, and it is a particularly interesting open question how improvisational constraints (i.e., the number of story elements) may impact creativity vs. cohesiveness (Tromp & Baer, 2022).
text.formatted: Here, we predict that more creative stories may have greater lexical diversity, more lexical categories, and more intense sentiment, and it is a particularly interesting open question how improvisational constraints (i.e., the number of story elements) may impact creativity vs. cohesiveness <ref type="bibr" target="#b88">(Tromp & Baer, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Finally, we tested language productivity metrics primarily as control variables so that we can isolate the meaningful effects of the other three categories.

We expect story length to predict creativity ratings, a well-documented but theoretically less interesting relationship (Taylor et al., 2021; Johnson et al., 2022; Forthmann et al., 2018; Kandemirci et al., 2025).
text.formatted: We expect story length to predict creativity ratings, a well-documented but theoretically less interesting relationship <ref type="bibr" target="#b86">(Taylor et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">Johnson et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Forthmann et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Kandemirci et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: We also expect readability to be more related to cohesiveness, given its relevance to the ease of narrative processing and comprehension.
All participants were fluent or native adult English speakers, located in the United States, with normal or corrected-to-normal hearing and vision, and access to a computer in a quiet environment.
This study was approved by the Research Subjects Review Board at the University of Rochester (STUDY00005470) under the OHSP and UR policies, and in accordance with
All participants gave informed consent before starting the study.
For storytellers, a working microphone was required.
In total, we originally recruited 100 storytellers via Prolific (https://prolific.com) to generate 6 stories each.
text.formatted: In total, we originally recruited 100 storytellers via Prolific (<ref type="url" target="https://prolific.com">https://prolific.com</ref>) to generate 6 stories each.

text.text: We plan to ultimately use this full corpus of stories to test multiple research questions, but due to financial and time constraints, for the purposes of the current study, we randomly selected 18 storytellers from the original 100, whose 6 stories each (a total of 108) were rated by experts and novices in this study (storyteller age: M = 43.67, SD = 13.97, range = 24-76; gender: 6 M, 12 F; ethnicity: 15 White/Caucasian, 1 Hispanic/Latino, 2 other; language: native = 17, fluent = 1).

We recruited 316 novice raters through Prolific (age: M = 36.32, SD = 11.73, range = 18-84; gender: 191 M, 107 F, 6 unspecified; ethnicity: 197 White/Caucasian, 35 Asian, 24 Black/African American, 17 Hispanic/Latino, 1 American Indian/Alaska Native, 30 other; language: native = 294, fluent = 10; 12 excluded due to data quality issues).

We also recruited 15 expert raters through the University of Rochester's English Department and Writing Center, and from online interest groups and listservs focused on creative writing and storytelling (age: M = 32.13, SD = 17.33, range = 21-70; gender: 4 M, 3 F, 8 unspecified; ethnicity: 8 White/Caucasian, 4 Asian, 1 Black/African American, 2 other; language: 10 native, 5 fluent).
These participants self-identified as having expertise in creative writing and storytelling, with experiences in publishing poetry, performing live storytelling, and being English professors.
Expertise research has traditionally faced two related methodological challenges due to the difficulty of recruiting experts.
First, expert samples are often small, which can reduce statistical power and decrease precision in parameter estimates (e.g., McAbee, 2018; Moreau, 2019).
text.formatted: First, expert samples are often small, which can reduce statistical power and decrease precision in parameter estimates (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">McAbee, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b64">Moreau, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Second, expert and novice groups are often substantially imbalanced in size (e.g., Kaufman et al., 2008 Kaufman et al., , 2009: 10 experts vs. 106 novices; Phonethibsavads et al., 2023: 3 experts vs. 19 novices; Hu et al., 2023: 3 experts vs. 21 novices).
text.formatted: Second, expert and novice groups are often substantially imbalanced in size (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Kaufman et al., 2008</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b46">Kaufman et al., , 2009</ref>: 10 experts vs. 106 novices; Phonethibsavads et al., 2023: 3 experts vs. 19 novices; <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Hu et al., 2023</ref>: 3 experts vs. 21 novices).

text.text: Here, we made our best effort to recruit a relatively large sample of experts (i.e., larger than most relevant previous work) and match them with comparable numbers of novice raters: each story was rated by 15 experts and 10-31 novices (M = 16.89, SD = 4.06).

Furthermore, our mixed-effects regression analyses modeled ratings at the story and rater level, allowing us to account for the different numbers of raters contributing to each story while directly testing the effects of expertise.

Each storyteller completed a story generation task through the online platform Labvanced (https://www.labvanced.com/) where they improvised six novel fictional stories (each three minutes long) based on six different prompts (story word count M = 405.48, SD = 77.07; descriptive data by prompt in Table S4).
text.formatted: Each storyteller completed a story generation task through the online platform Labvanced (<ref type="url" target="https://www.labvanced.com/">https://www.labvanced.com/</ref>) where they improvised six novel fictional stories (each three minutes long) based on six different prompts (story word count M = 405.48, SD = 77.07; descriptive data by prompt in Table <ref type="table">S4</ref>).

text.text: Each prompt contained one to three random elements.
Example prompts included: "a pet snake," "a locked box and a love song," and "an abandoned house and a birthday card."
They were given the same sentence with which to start and end each story.
Human raters scored several dimensions for 108 stories, told by 18 storytellers, each of whom created one story for each of the six prompts.
Raters were given story transcripts rather than raw audio recordings (see Data Preprocessing) to eliminate effects of speech acoustics.
Both expert and novice raters were given the same instructions for story evaluation.

They were informed that the stories were transcripts of spoken narratives improvised in response to a given prompt, without knowing the specific prompt content or the number of elements in each prompt.

We applied the Consensual Assessment Technique (Amabile, 1982) and instructed participants to use their own definitions and subjective judgment to rate each story across five narrative dimensions, informed by previous work on creative assessment and narrative evaluation: creativity, imagination, novelty, complexity, and cohesiveness (e.g., creativity: How creative is the story?) (e.g., Amabile, 1982; Hennessey & Amabile, 1988; Runco & Jaeger, 2012; Patel et al., 2025).
text.formatted: We applied the Consensual Assessment Technique <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Amabile, 1982)</ref> and instructed participants to use their own definitions and subjective judgment to rate each story across five narrative dimensions, informed by previous work on creative assessment and narrative evaluation: creativity, imagination, novelty, complexity, and cohesiveness (e.g., creativity: How creative is the story?) (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Amabile, 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Hennessey & Amabile, 1988;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Runco & Jaeger, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Patel et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: No examples or practice phases were provided to avoid influencing raters' judgments, consistent with prior studies (e.g., Amabile, 1982; Kaufman et al., 2007; Kaufman et al., 2008).
text.formatted: No examples or practice phases were provided to avoid influencing raters' judgments, consistent with prior studies (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Amabile, 1982;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b49">Kaufman et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Kaufman et al., 2008)</ref>.

text.text: Ratings were made on a scale from 1 (low) to 5 (high), and both stories and rating dimensions were presented in randomized order.
Raters were instructed to use the full rating scale and flip between questions and stories to revise their ratings as needed, and complete the survey in one setting in a quiet environment.

Because each story was relatively long and the study included a large number of stories, a multi-session design was necessary for expert raters to evaluate a subset of stories in each session to minimize fatigue and ensure data quality.
Expert raters each completed six sessions of story evaluations on Qualtrics (https://www.qualtrics.com/).
text.formatted: Expert raters each completed six sessions of story evaluations on Qualtrics (<ref type="url" target="https://www.qualtrics.com/">https://www.qualtrics.com/</ref>).

text.text: In each session, they rated 18 stories, which were based on six different prompts.
Each prompt had three stories randomly drawn from different storytellers.
Sessions were presented in a randomized order for each rater, and each story received ratings from 15 different expert raters.
In contrast, a multi-session design was less suitable for novice raters, who were recruited online to maintain a diverse and heterogeneous participant pool.

Multi-session online studies are associated with higher attrition rates (Rodd, 2024), and based on our lab's prior experience it would have been very difficult to find online participants through Prolific to complete all sessions.
text.formatted: Multi-session online studies are associated with higher attrition rates <ref type="bibr" target="#b78">(Rodd, 2024)</ref>, and based on our lab's prior experience it would have been very difficult to find online participants through Prolific to complete all sessions.

text.text: Therefore, we used a modified rating procedure for novices.
Novice raters completed a single session on Labvanced where they rated six randomly selected stories from the full set of 108.
These stories were chosen from different speakers and prompts to ensure diversity.
The stories were presented in a randomized order, and each story received ratings from between 10 and 31 novice raters (M = 16.89, SD = 4.06).
Importantly, we conducted rigorous control analyses and found no evidence that the differences in session structure between experts and novices confounded the findings of the study (Table S8).
text.formatted: Importantly, we conducted rigorous control analyses and found no evidence that the differences in session structure between experts and novices confounded the findings of the study (Table <ref type="table">S8</ref>).

text.text: Story recordings were transcribed in Descript (https://www.descript.com/), an automated transcription software.
text.formatted: Story recordings were transcribed in Descript (<ref type="url" target="https://www.descript.com/">https://www.descript.com/</ref>), an automated transcription software.

text.text: These transcripts were then manually cleaned by research assistants to correct spelling and punctuation errors, and eliminate irrelevant or disfluent segments (e.g., false starts like "Tom [wrong name] is going to… Mary [correct name] is going to…" or self-corrections such as "oh sorry I'll start this sentence again").
Filler words (e.g., um, uh) were also removed from texts.

Descript's automated transcription was generally accurate (>90%), but additional cues like falling intonation and pauses greater than two seconds were used to determine sentence boundaries in run-on sentences.
text.formatted: Descript's automated transcription was generally accurate (>90%), but additional cues like falling intonation and pauses greater than two seconds were used to determine sentence boundaries in run-on sentences.

text.text: The goal of using cleaned transcripts, rather than audio recordings or the raw transcripts, was to isolate the literal narrative content and minimize the influence of acoustic features and unrelated meta-commentaries on raters' judgments.
Cleaned transcripts helped raters focus on core story elements like character development and narrative structure while generally maintaining the style of spoken language.
We derived four categories of linguistic and structural features from the cleaned story transcripts: semantic similarity, lexical predictability, lexical composition, and language productivity.
Semantic Similarity.

Our first set of metrics was based on similarity between semantic embeddings, or vectorized multidimensional representations of the distributional properties of a given token (Turney & Pantel, 2010), to capture the relatedness between words and between sentences.
text.formatted: Our first set of metrics was based on similarity between semantic embeddings, or vectorized multidimensional representations of the distributional properties of a given token <ref type="bibr" target="#b89">(Turney & Pantel, 2010)</ref>, to capture the relatedness between words and between sentences.

text.text: Specifically, we generated contextualized word embeddings from the final layer of a transformer model, Longformer (Beltagy et al., 2020), which can take relatively long documents (e.g., stories) as input, compared to similar contextual models.
text.formatted: Specifically, we generated contextualized word embeddings from the final layer of a transformer model, Longformer <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Beltagy et al., 2020)</ref>, which can take relatively long documents (e.g., stories) as input, compared to similar contextual models.

text.text: Using these embeddings, we computed metrics to quantify word-level similarity (mean and standard deviation across all word pairs).
At the sentence-level, we tracked individual word tokens within each sentence and excluded special model tokens (e.g., <s>, </s>, <pad>).
text.formatted: At the sentence-level, we tracked individual word tokens within each sentence and excluded special model tokens (e.g., <s>, </s>, <pad>).

text.text: We then averaged token embeddings within each sentence to generate representative sentence-level embedding vectors (Arora et al., 2017; White et al., 2015), which were used to compute sentence-level similarity metrics (between the first and the last sentence; mean and standard deviation across all sentence pairs and across all adjacent sentence pairs); see Figure 3A for computational process.
text.formatted: We then averaged token embeddings within each sentence to generate representative sentence-level embedding vectors <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Arora et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b92">White et al., 2015)</ref>, which were used to compute sentence-level similarity metrics (between the first and the last sentence; mean and standard deviation across all sentence pairs and across all adjacent sentence pairs); see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_2">3A</ref> for computational process.

text.text: Although storytellers were instructed to start and end a story with highly similar phrasings, the embeddings for those sentences (which incorporate context) represent different meanings due to different overall story content; the first-to-last sentence similarity metric thus reflects the global semantic structure of a story, despite local textual similarity.

We utilized a pre-trained language model, GPT-2 Large (774M parameters; Radford et al., 2019), to generate token probabilities, which were then used to calculate surprisal and entropy for each token for each story.
text.formatted: We utilized a pre-trained language model, GPT-2 Large (774M parameters; <ref type="bibr" target="#b73">Radford et al., 2019)</ref>, to generate token probabilities, which were then used to calculate surprisal and entropy for each token for each story.

text.text: For both surprisal and entropy, we computed the mean to capture the overall story predictability, as well as standard deviation to capture how uniform or dynamic information is distributed.
Surprisal quantifies how unexpected a specific token is in each context, defined as the negative log-probability of a token given its preceding context (Hale, 2001; Eq. S1).
text.formatted: Surprisal quantifies how unexpected a specific token is in each context, defined as the negative log-probability of a token given its preceding context <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Hale, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Eq. S1)</ref>.

text.text: Entropy, on the other hand, quantifies the level of uncertainty about a particular word position given prior context.
Specifically, entropy is defined as the expected surprisal over all tokens in the model's vocabulary and is associated with longer reading time (Van Schijndel & Linzen, 2018; Eq. S4).
text.formatted: Specifically, entropy is defined as the expected surprisal over all tokens in the model's vocabulary and is associated with longer reading time <ref type="bibr" target="#b90">(Van Schijndel & Linzen, 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr">Eq. S4)</ref>.

text.text: Lexical Composition.
This category captures linguistic-emotional expressiveness and the improvisational demands of a story.
It includes the number of lexical categories, calculated using Empath (Fast et al., 2016), which classifies words into over 200 pre-validated semantic categories.
text.formatted: It includes the number of lexical categories, calculated using Empath <ref type="bibr">(Fast et al., 2016)</ref>, which classifies words into over 200 pre-validated semantic categories.

text.text: We also calculated lexical diversity using the type-token ratio (number of unique tokens divided by the total number of tokens; Richards, 1987), and emotionality using the VADER sentiment lexicon (Hutto & Gilbert, 2014), with absolute values of normalized, weighted compound sentiment scores ranging from 0 (least intense) to 1 (most intense).
text.formatted: We also calculated lexical diversity using the type-token ratio (number of unique tokens divided by the total number of tokens; <ref type="bibr" target="#b77">Richards, 1987)</ref>, and emotionality using the VADER sentiment lexicon <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Hutto & Gilbert, 2014)</ref>, with absolute values of normalized, weighted compound sentiment scores ranging from 0 (least intense) to 1 (most intense).

text.text: The number of random story elements (e.g., "a pet snake"; "a locked box") in the given prompt was also included to capture the degree of improvisational constraint of the story.

Individual metrics in this feature category measure the mere quantity of text, including total word count, sentence count, mean length of utterance (MLU), and the Flesch Readability Score (a score based on sentence length and word syllable complexity, ranging from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating greater ease of reading).
These metrics serve as coarse indicators of baseline verbal fluency, syntactic complexity, and linguistic clarity.
Metrics that significantly predict human ratings in this category will be used as control variables when evaluating metrics from the other three categories.

We first ran linear mixed-effects models to see whether experts and novices differ in their story ratings, using lme4 (Bates et al., 2015) and lmerTest (Kuznetsova et al., 2017) packages in R. Models included by-story and by-rater random intercepts to account for item-level and subject-level baseline differences.

Models included by-story and by-rater random intercepts to account for item-level and subject-level baseline differences.

text.text: Next, to examine the multidimensional structure of the rating space, we conducted Principal Component Analysis (PCA) using the FactoMineR (Lê et al., 2008) package in R. We also used linear mixed-effects models with the same random structure to examine group differences in the relationships among rating dimensions and links between rating dimensions and linguistic features.
text.formatted: Next, to examine the multidimensional structure of the rating space, we conducted Principal Component Analysis (PCA) using the FactoMineR <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Lê et al., 2008)</ref> package in R. We also used linear mixed-effects models with the same random structure to examine group differences in the relationships among rating dimensions and links between rating dimensions and linguistic features.

text.text: The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995) was applied to correct for multiple testing each time we examined a main effect (i.e., whether a linguistic feature in the semantic similarity, lexical predictability, or lexical composition categories significantly predicted human ratings).
text.formatted: The Benjamini-Hochberg procedure <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995)</ref> was applied to correct for multiple testing each time we examined a main effect (i.e., whether a linguistic feature in the semantic similarity, lexical predictability, or lexical composition categories significantly predicted human ratings).

text.text: Moderation analyses were then restricted to metrics with significant main effects and used a significance level of α = 0.05.
All other statistical tests were also conducted at α = 0.05.

To account for potential practice effects arising from experts rating more stories across multiple sessions than novices, we conducted supplementary analyses (Table S8), which indicated that such effects are unlikely to explain the reported expertise differences.

text.text: We include a detailed description of the analyses and findings under "Control Analysis" below.

text.text: First, we tested whether experts' and novices' mean ratings differ significantly along five narrative dimensions (creativity, imagination, novelty, complexity, cohesiveness).

We ran a linear mixed-effects model to examine whether ratings differed by rater group across the five dimensions, including rater group, dimension, and their interaction as fixed effects, with random intercepts for rater and story.
We found no significant main effect of rater group on overall ratings across dimensions (β = -0.12, SE = 0.15, p = 0.424) (Figure 1A).
text.formatted: We found no significant main effect of rater group on overall ratings across dimensions (β = -0.12, SE = 0.15, p = 0.424) (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1A</ref>).

text.text: There was a significant interaction between rater group and dimension, and post-hoc simple effects comparisons showed that this was driven by complexity, with experts giving higher complexity ratings than novices (β = -0.40, SE = 0.16, p = 0.010).

In contrast, the two groups' ratings did not differ significantly for creativity (β = -0.05, SE = 0.16, p = 0.732), imagination (β = -0.07, SE = 0.16, p = 0.673), novelty (β = -0.09, SE = 0.16, p = 0.582), or cohesiveness (β = 0.12, SE = 0.16, p = 0.423) (All five post-hoc tests above were Bonferroni corrected).
Second, to understand the overall structure of the story rating space, we performed Principal Component Analysis (PCA) on ratings from each group.

We identified two optimal principal components in the rating space for both experts and novices by visually inspecting the scree plot using the "elbow" method (Figure S1A -B; Cattell, 1966; Sen & Cohen, 2025).
text.formatted: We identified two optimal principal components in the rating space for both experts and novices by visually inspecting the scree plot using the "elbow" method (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">S1A</ref> <ref type="bibr">-B;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Cattell, 1966;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b80">Sen & Cohen, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Analysis of the contributions of each rating dimension to the principal components revealed that, for both groups, the first component reflected a strongly overlapping concept of creativity, novelty, imagination, and complexity, while the other one substantially reflected cohesiveness (Figure 1B).
text.formatted: Analysis of the contributions of each rating dimension to the principal components revealed that, for both groups, the first component reflected a strongly overlapping concept of creativity, novelty, imagination, and complexity, while the other one substantially reflected cohesiveness (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1B</ref>).

text.text: This pattern is consistent with Patel et al. (2025), in which they found creativity and coherence to reflect distinct dimensions of spontaneous speech.
text.formatted: This pattern is consistent with <ref type="bibr" target="#b69">Patel et al. (2025)</ref>, in which they found creativity and coherence to reflect distinct dimensions of spontaneous speech.

text.text: Although the overall structure of the rating space was quite similar across groups, we wondered whether the more fine-grained relationships between these five rating dimensions of narrative quality might still differ.

To statistically test for potential differences between the pattern of correlation between dimensions, we used linear mixed-effect models predicting each story dimension with another story dimension, rater group, and their interaction term, with by-rater and by-story random intercepts (e.g., Figure 1C).
text.formatted: To statistically test for potential differences between the pattern of correlation between dimensions, we used linear mixed-effect models predicting each story dimension with another story dimension, rater group, and their interaction term, with by-rater and by-story random intercepts (e.g., Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1C</ref>).

text.text: We found that although creativity, imagination, and novelty were significantly correlated in both experts and novices (Figure 1D; see Table S1 for full results), there was a significant interaction between these associations and rater group, indicating that experts had weaker associations between rating dimensions.
text.formatted: We found that although creativity, imagination, and novelty were significantly correlated in both experts and novices (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1D</ref>; see Table <ref type="table">S1</ref> for full results), there was a significant interaction between these associations and rater group, indicating that experts had weaker associations between rating dimensions.

text.text: Specifically, this interaction with rater group was significant for the association between creativity and novelty (interaction: β = -0.17, SE = 0.03, p < 0.001; Figure 1C), creativity and imagination (β = -0.19, SE = 0.02, p < 0.001), novelty and imagination (β = -0.13, SE = 0.03, p < 0.001), and complexity and novelty (β = -0.09, SE = 0.03, p = 0.008).
text.formatted: Specifically, this interaction with rater group was significant for the association between creativity and novelty (interaction: β = -0.17, SE = 0.03, p < 0.001; Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_0">1C</ref>), creativity and imagination (β = -0.19, SE = 0.02, p < 0.001), novelty and imagination (β = -0.13, SE = 0.03, p < 0.001), and complexity and novelty (β = -0.09, SE = 0.03, p = 0.008).

text.text: Additionally, we ruled out the possibility that experts' weaker associations were simply due to less consistent ratings than novices.
We compared the internal consistency of ratings for experts and novices using Cronbach's alpha, with shuffled ratings serving as a baseline for comparison.
Both experts' and novices' ratings were more internally consistent than shuffled ratings, while their internal reliability did not significantly differ from each other.
Thus, the weaker associations among experts were unlikely to reflect lower rating consistency (see Table S2 and Figure S2).
text.formatted: Thus, the weaker associations among experts were unlikely to reflect lower rating consistency (see Table <ref type="table">S2</ref> and Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">S2</ref>).

text.text: Overall, these results indicate that experts have more distinct representations of several of these story dimensions, suggesting a more nuanced rating space overall, compared to novices. all 108 stories.

The results above suggest that, while experts and novices rate improvised stories similarly overall, they diverge in terms of more fine-grained associations between individual story dimensions.
Next, we tested the hypothesis that experts' and novices' ratings may be driven by different linguistic features of stories.

We included four categories of metrics: language productivity (overall quantity of content in a story, which we primarily used as a control), semantic similarity, lexical predictability (how expected or surprising a story is), and lexical composition (e.g., the diversity and emotionality of words).

Since PCA revealed two distinct, latent components of ratings, we decided to run regression models on two individual story dimensions which were highly representative of each component (i.e., cohesiveness and creativity, the latter of which was highly correlated with novelty, imagination, and complexity; Figures 1B & 1D).

Next, we report the full model with all relevant metrics predicting story ratings to assess their relative contribution to human ratings and qualitatively compare the contributions of experts and novices.

text.text: As predicted, stories that had higher word and sentence counts were rated as more creative (β = 0.10, SE = 0.04, p = 0.006; β = 0.08, SE = 0.04, p = 0.039, respectively) but not more cohesive (β = 0.05, SE = 0.03, p = 0.184; β = -0.03, SE = 0.03, p = 0.422, respectively).
On the other hand, stories with longer MLU were rated as more cohesive but not more creative (β = 0.08, SE = 0.03, p = 0.016; β = 0.002, SE = 0.04, p = 0.942, respectively).

This pattern of results converges with our PCA findings, such that creativity and cohesiveness are two related but conceptually distinct aspects of overall story quality, driven by different text characteristics.
Readability was not associated with any of the story dimensions, possibly due to a ceiling effect such that all stories are easily readable (see Table S3).

text.text: Because experts and novices had different survey structures (i.e., each expert completed six sessions, whereas each novice completed one session only), we conducted an additional analysis to see whether the observed expertise effects could be driven by experts completing more sessions and rating more stories, rather than by true expertise differences.
We focused on results that showed significant group differences.

We directly tested the influence of session by running polynomial mixed-effects regression models to test whether inter-dimension relationships and feature-to-rating relationships changed across expert sessions (modeled as a second-order polynomial with by-story and by-rater random intercepts).

No significant linear or quadratic trends were observed across sessions (Table S8), indicating that the reported group differences cannot be explained by differences in task exposure or practice effects between experts and novices.

text.text: Finally, to directly compare the relative impact of different metrics on story ratings, we entered all significant metrics above into the same model (one model for creativity, one for cohesiveness), while controlling for word count, sentence count, and MLU, with by-story and by-rater random intercepts (Figure 5).

text.text: For creativity, results showed that for both rater groups, the first-to-last sentence similarity metric had the largest effect, followed by lexical diversity.
As for cohesiveness, the first-to-last sentence similarity metric was also the strongest predictor for both groups.
Additionally, the number of story elements predicted novices' cohesiveness ratings (but not experts').

Moreover, although we were unable to systematically test whether coefficient magnitudes differed significantly between groups due to constraints of model convergence, the overall pattern suggests that magnitude tended to be smaller for experts than for novices.
Taken together, these results suggest that first-to-last semantic similarity is an important signature of both creativity and cohesiveness.
Lexical diversity was a significant predictor of creativity only, and this pattern was observed in both groups.
Stories improvised under greater constraints (i.e., with a larger number of elements) were rated as less cohesive, particularly by novices.

Overall, while experts and novices were influenced by similar linguistic features, novices relied more heavily on these features when evaluating both creativity and cohesiveness. predicted creativity or cohesiveness.
